A veteran's plan, for the ones still fighting the war after the war

No More Folded Flags.

There is a tool — backed by peer-reviewed clinical trials — that helps veterans quiet the noise of PTSD in weeks, not decades. The VA already acknowledges it. But there's no way to get it to the tens of thousands who need it. This is the plan to fix that.

By Linda — disabled veteran, military spouse, founder of a service-disabled-veteran-owned consulting firm. Someone who has been in the dark place, and came back.

If you're a veteran in crisis right now:

Call 988, then press 1 — or text 838255. The Veterans Crisis Line is free, confidential, and staffed 24/7, many by fellow veterans. You don't need to be enrolled in VA care. Please reach out.

A month ago, a soldier under my husband's command took his own life.

He was 34. A wife. A 15-year-old daughter. A 5-year-old daughter. He served in Afghanistan and Iraq for half a dozen years, and he carried significant PTSD home with him.

Within five days, my husband had to drop everything and stand at that funeral. And the support this family got amounted to "thank you for your service."

Here's the flag. It's all over. This is what you get for your husband's service: a folded piece of cloth. His body is in the ground, and you're going to have to figure out how to make whatever you can of your life.

The daughter hugged my husband and cried in his arms. It broke his heart. It should break all of ours.

It tore my husband up for weeks. He was blown away by how mature that 15-year-old was — she hugged him and just started crying. Her dad was gone. And that's how it ended for him.

"I never want there to be another five-year-old girl standing beside her sister wondering — why isn't Dad here? Why did my world end?"— Linda

He didn't lack courage. He lacked tools.

That man survived six years of war. What he didn't have, on the worst night of his life, was a way to see where the light was at the end of the tunnel — a way to get through the dark moment.

I know, because I've been in that dark place myself. I've been hospitalized in VA hospitals. I know the trauma where you want to curl up on the floor because it feels so bad you don't know how you'll get through it.

There is a way through it. And it isn't "tough it out." And it isn't a prescription and a pat on the back — pharmacology alone is a band-aid that never touches the root.

The bridges that collapsed aren't the veteran's fault. Nobody ever built them a real one.
Lean into the science

Does tapping work? Yes.

EFT — Emotional Freedom Techniques, "tapping" — is not a wellness fad. It is one of the most-studied brief interventions for veteran PTSD, and the results embarrass almost everything else:

  • 86% of veterans no longer met clinical PTSD criteria after just six sessions.Randomized controlled trial, Church et al., Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease (2013). Gains held at 6-month follow-up. Read the study →
  • An independent replication trial found the same thing.A second randomized controlled trial replicated the result in 2017 — this isn't one lucky study. See the replication →
  • The VA itself approved EFT as a generally safe therapy in 2017.The door is already cracked open. Somebody just has to walk through it with a plan. The story →
  • It measurably changes the body, not just the mood.Cortisol, resting heart rate, blood pressure, and anxiety markers all improved in clinical EFT studies. Physiological markers study →

And here's what I know from 44 years of trying everything else: counseling, pharmaceuticals, "just meditate." This is the one thing that actually let me feel comfortable in my own skin. I want that for every veteran who's faking it, shiny on the outside, stuck in survival on the inside.

The problem isn't the tool. It's the delivery system.

The VA's Veterans Stress Project is real and it's good — it recognized EFT as a valid way to treat PTSD. But look closer: it's a patchwork of individual practitioners and one-off discounts. One coach in a rowboat, on an ocean of people who need help.

There is no scalability. No way to mass-deliver it inside the VA system. Because it was never set up that way.

Was everyone going to get in the life raft? No. But we can put a raft within arm's reach of every single one.

That's what changes everything: modular, self-serve tapping programs — video modules a veteran can open at 2 a.m. when the dark moment hits — backed by live coaching, measured like a clinical program, delivered at the scale of software.

The plan

You don't convince the VA. You show the VA.

Nobody wins an argument with a bureaucracy. But nobody argues with results either. So we start small — deliberately small:

The pilot is the key. Proof opens doors that pitches never will.

Step 1 — Pilot. Small cohorts in Indianapolis, New York, and San Diego. Veterans go through a structured tapping program: modules plus coaching.

Step 2 — Proof. Measure everything the VA already measures: PTSD symptom scores, sleep, medication load, sense of purpose. Compare. Let the numbers talk.

Step 3 — The door opens. Walk into the VA not with a pitch but with a working, scalable program and data from their own population. Then grow it — because veterans are one population, and there are so many others waiting behind them.

And I'm the right person to walk it in. I'm a disabled veteran. My husband is active duty. My firm is a certified Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business on a GSA schedule — I've spent my career getting things through government doors. I know how to talk to this population, because I am this population.

Linda's next idea — and it's a big one

Build the engine once. Help every population.

Here's the insight Linda had that turns this from a program into a movement: with AI, you can build EFT modules fast — and tailor each one to the population and the issue it serves.

"You could make EFT modules so easily… we need it for this population, focused on this issue — tailored to the women, to the men. You could do so many different things with it." — Linda

A module for combat PTSD. A module for women veterans. For the spouse who's holding the family together. For sleep. For the transition out of uniform, when purpose evaporates. Each one in the language of the people it serves — built in days, not years, and refined by the coaches who use them.

One engine. Endless rafts.

For Linda — take it further

Ten questions to build on

  1. Which VA relationships do you already have warm access to — and who is the ONE person who could greenlight a small pilot?
  2. What would the VA need to see from a pilot to take it seriously — which metrics do their own programs get judged on?
  3. Could the first cohort run entirely outside the VA (veteran nonprofits, VSOs, base family-readiness groups) so no bureaucratic approval can slow it down?
  4. Britt's program is the engine you know works. What's the minimum module set for a veterans pilot — and what has to be adapted for military culture and language?
  5. Who measures the results so they're credible — is there a university or research partner (the EFT research community is active) who'd co-author the outcome data?
  6. Your SDVOSB certification opens contracting doors. Is the long-term play a VA contract, a nonprofit funded by donors, or both running side by side?
  7. Which population is pilot #2 — women veterans, military spouses, first responders, Gold Star families?
  8. What would a "2 a.m. module" look like — the one a veteran opens alone on the worst night? Who reviews it for crisis-safety?
  9. Your GovCon friends in DC: which three should hear this story first, and what exactly do you want each one to do?
  10. What does this look like in five years if it works — and what would you need to be true of YOUR life for you to lead it that long without burning out?
